A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RAM study. All 15 pages, including supplementary Sections A–E, are readable, and the equations, tables, figures, and appendix content can be reliably matched.

before.justification: v1 reports original object-detection experiments, architectural ablations, synthetic noise and weather evaluations, and additional experiments in the supplement.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and adds a comparison of separate versus joint training across four datasets in Appendix B.3.

M1.justification: The parallel ISP operations, shared parameter encoder, separate decoders, feature fusion, normalization, and detection-loss training remain unchanged. The RAM and RAM-T architectures also match across the renumbered appendix tables.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same seven RAW benchmark subsets and synthetic noise and weather scenarios. Appendix B.3 reuses PASCALRAW, NOD-Nikon, NOD-Sony, and LOD-Dark under joint training without adding datasets, tasks, or unseen-sensor evaluations.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in the retained experiments, including the main benchmark and frozen-detector comparisons. DynamicISP receives revised scores but remains the same comparator; the new appendix experiment compares RAM training configurations.

E3.justification: New Appendix B.3 compares dataset-specific models with one model jointly trained on four existing datasets. This adds an evaluation design; previously documented detector choices, preprocessing, optimization schedules, and metrics remain unchanged. The new experiment does not specify its detector or detailed training configuration.

E4.justification: Appendix B.3 adds an analysis of whether pooling heterogeneous RAW datasets benefits RAM relative to separate training. Figure 4 also gains ground-truth references and a revised RAM prediction example. Existing ablations, robustness tests, and supplementary analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version specifies repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests for the reported comparisons. v2 adds and revises point estimates without changing uncertainty-reporting practices.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises DynamicISP mAP from 31.3 to 32.0 on LOD-Dark, 35.3 to 37.0 on LOD-Normal, 38.3 to 41.4 on ROD-Night, and 28.2 to 30.1 on NOD-Nikon, with corresponding mAP50 updates. Table 2 repeats the revised ROD-Night score and adds absolute baseline costs. New Table 9 reports separate/joint-training mAP of 67.7/69.6, 31.9/32.8, 32.8/35.8, and 48.0/48.2 on its four datasets. Figure 4 changes RAM's ROD-Night predictions. Existing aggregate RAM scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The ISP transformations in Equations 1–5 and the Shapley contribution formula in Section 4.6 are unchanged. No formal assumptions, propositions, proofs, or derivations are added or revised.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about parallel RAW processing, detection performance, efficiency, and architectural flexibility. The added appendix evidence does not redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix B.3 interprets joint-training gains as evidence that adaptive processing handles heterogeneous sensor distributions. Appendix E changes the tentative belief that diverse-sensor training could address generalization limitations into an assertion supported by B.3. That experiment evaluates included datasets, so transfer to unseen sensors remains unestablished.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link in the abstract. Table 2 newly specifies the RAW/ResNet18 baseline's 12.3 million parameters and 35.8 ms inference time. Existing architecture and optimization details are retained; these disclosures do not establish implementation changes.

R1.justification: Both versions cite the same 58 works and retain the same related-work discussion and positioning against sequential ISP approaches. Reference movement and changed citation page locators are presentational.

P1.justification: v2 adds Appendix B.3, makes small introductory wording edits, updates the affiliation from Sony AI to Sony Research, and adjusts cross-references. The overall narrative and section organization remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds Table 9, renumbers the former Tables 9–10 as Tables 10–11, adds a ground-truth column to Figure 4, and labels the dataset rows in Figure 6. Several tables and surrounding paragraphs shift position, while the overall two-column layout is retained.

improvement.justification: v2 adds useful evidence about joint training on heterogeneous RAW datasets, provides code-access information and absolute baseline costs, and makes qualitative comparisons easier to assess through ground-truth images and dataset labels. These are limited improvements to evidence and transparency. The new experiment lacks important setup details and does not establish unseen-sensor transfer, limiting the support for the stronger generalization wording in Appendix E.
